A drone $D$ takes off from a point $P$ and flies at a constant angle of ${45}^{∘}$ to the horizontal. How fast is the drone gaining altitude if its speed is $42\,\text{km/h}?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/40/40e0ae889d241c45464492ba3842d586effe528ab93b3554f6dbfb01d215c308.png)

Let $y$ be the drone's altitude and $z$ be the actual distance between the drone and its take-off point, as shown below.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={45}^{∘},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({45}^{∘}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ y & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=42\,\text{km/h}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot 42=21\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the altitude is increasing at a rate of $21\sqrt{2}\,\text{km/h}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "![](images/d4/d486581ea48bc96adc1269fbf40d1d71a547e92977f71e3a74336a147ef9b222.png)

A potato $P$ is fired from a cannon $C$ at an angle of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ radians from the horizontal. The horizontal distance the projectile travels increases at a rate of $18\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$ If the angle of elevation does not change, what is the speed of the potato?" :question/worked-solution "![](images/8b/8b5af04f58fe65b46adaae47d97b857d1e8765122a811179cf25ba22733e6415.png)

Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from the potato to the cannon and $z$ be the actual distance between them, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ z & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}x) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=18\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot 18=12\sqrt{3}.
$$

A drone $D$ is approaching a landing point $L$ on the ground at an angle of $\frac{\pi }{4}$ radians to the horizontal. The drone's shadow $S$ is projected onto the ground vertically below the drone. If the drone is approaching the ground with a speed of $6\,\text{ft}/\text{s},$ what is the speed of the drone's shadow?" :question/worked-solution "![](images/9c/9cb94ea5cab43d48da6b836026d302504d7e63fe1260aa81a2b577436b6b4e98.png)

Let $x$ be the distance between the landing point and the shadow, and let $z$ be the distance between the landing point and the drone, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ x & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=-6\,\text{ft}/\text{s}$ (negative because the distance between the landing point and the drone is decreasing). Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot (-6)=-3\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the speed of the shadow is $3\sqrt{2}\,\text{ft/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186063486 :answer-field/correct "answer-a65dd8fb-bbd1-58b7-ac02-a42d4c6ccf90" :answer-field/choices ["answer-329a50a1-1867-5bec-a6de-7ff85577816f" "answer-a65dd8fb-bbd1-58b7-ac02-a42d4c6ccf90" "answer-66fcb494-c0d9-5ffb-979e-79b874aa5657" "answer-2f5ba0a7-0f58-5b5c-822b-751a3fca36dc" "answer-a74ae6ab-9a62-5384-a6ec-5a1fa233a9c8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-329a50a1-1867-5bec-a6de-7ff85577816f" :answer/id #uuid "329a50a1-1867-5bec-a6de-7ff85577816f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\,\text{ft/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a65dd8fb-bbd1-58b7-ac02-a42d4c6ccf90" :answer/id #uuid "a65dd8fb-bbd1-58b7-ac02-a42d4c6ccf90" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}\,\text{ft/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-66fcb494-c0d9-5ffb-979e-79b874aa5657" :answer/id #uuid "66fcb494-c0d9-5ffb-979e-79b874aa5657" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\sqrt{3}\,\text{ft/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2f5ba0a7-0f58-5b5c-822b-751a3fca36dc" :answer/id #uuid "2f5ba0a7-0f58-5b5c-822b-751a3fca36dc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{2}\,\text{ft/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a74ae6ab-9a62-5384-a6ec-5a1fa233a9c8" :answer/id #uuid "a74ae6ab-9a62-5384-a6ec-5a1fa233a9c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{3}\,\text{ft/s}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c70a238b-9801-5892-a5eb-17f62e1925f8" :question/id #uuid "c70a238b-9801-5892-a5eb-17f62e1925f8" :question/math-academy-id "q-121348" :question/problem "![](images/5e/5e96676aca66b99fd1e080d6c0cbbe79a5197125a3bcc8f04e67ca406947af10.png)

A bullet $B$ is fired from a cannon $C$ at an angle of ${60}^{∘}$ from the horizontal. Given that the bullet's horizontal speed is $300\,\text{ft}/\text{s},$ calculate the actual speed of the bullet in the direction it is traveling." :question/worked-solution "![](images/fe/fea05a36487813579d4633d9134bdd1d8c4d4bef4e9f57ba997b7b8715d46f32.png)

Let $x$ denote the horizontal distance from the bullet's projection to the cannon, and $z$ be the distance between the bullet and the cannon, as shown above.

We want to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ={60}^{∘},$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡({60}^{∘}) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{x}{z} \\ z & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(z) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2x) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =2\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=300\text{ft}/\text{s}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=2\cdot 300=600.
$$

Therefore, the speed of the plane is $600\,\text{ft}/\text{s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0f706d85-4abb-551b-ac2a-41285f5f5b00"] :db/ensure A car $C$ drives toward a $108\,\text{m}$ high building $B$ following a straight path. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the car and the top of the building $T$ is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\pi }{36}$ radians per second. What is the speed of the car when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/f2/f28ca3385d2179984c29d27a06926806e445c1dbab2cfa5f9fd6857149b632bb.png)

  

In the figure, $x$ is the distance between the car and the building, and $y$ is the building's height. The quantity $y=108$ meters does not change with time because the building's height is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{y} \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{108} \\ x & =108\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(108\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-108{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{\pi }{36}$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{3}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-108{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}))\frac{\pi }{36} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-108{(\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3})}^{2}\frac{\pi }{36} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-3\pi (\frac{4}{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-4\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the car is $4\pi \,\text{m/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c764bd62-dac9-5c30-b3ea-6e5444aa2fdd"] :db/ensure A lighthouse $L$ shines a beam that hits the surface of the sea at point $B.$ The light is mounted at a height of $10\,\text{m}$ above the water. As the beam is tilted downward, the angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the beam and the point $B$ is increasing at a rate of $0.12$ radians per second. What is the speed of the light spot as a function of $\theta ?$ 

*Hint*: Remember that speed is always positive or zero.

The speed of the light spot is 
{{field-1}}
$\text{m/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/bd/bd5afbe33a3a82ec439c5807aa99d1d28639ed74126c2dd483093ca511b253c9.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the height of the lighthouse above the water, and $x$ is the horizontal distance from the lighthouse base to the light spot on the water. The quantity $y=10$ meters does not change with time because the light’s height is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{10}{x} \\ x & =\frac{10}{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } \\ x & =10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=0.12.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-10{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )(0.12) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.2{csc}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the light spot toward the lighthouse is $1.2{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{m/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7c8015e3-4339-5833-a2d3-370dba776e3b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7c8015e3-4339-5833-a2d3-370dba776e3b" :answer-field/id #uuid "7c8015e3-4339-5833-a2d3-370dba776e3b" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-cc2bd856-1319-532a-a82f-52ad02474213" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cc2bd856-1319-532a-a82f-52ad02474213"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cc2bd856-1319-532a-a82f-52ad02474213" :answer/id #uuid "cc2bd856-1319-532a-a82f-52ad02474213" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.2\csc^{2}(\theta)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-8512c354-4d05-539a-b5eb-ac69014916bb" :question/id #uuid "8512c354-4d05-539a-b5eb-ac69014916bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-83679" :question/problem "![](images/d2/d2e2666baf2931dc4e0d8ba097a364b7b7a1bba75e65c8d802a60180e9a94854.png)

Neah is flying a kite $K$ with a string of length $112\,\text{ft}.$ The angle of elevation $\theta $ of the kite is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\pi }{28}$ radians per second. Find, as a function of $\theta ,$ the rate at which the kite's altitude is increasing." :question/worked-solution "![](images/8c/8c3c9e40f56d0b269562c37fd2d87c7e8f0394c8f55dca596e5e751f5e96157b.png)

  

In the figure, $y$ is the altitude of the kite, and $z$ is the distance between the kite and Neah. The quantity $z=112\,\text{ft}$ does not change with time because the kite string's length is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{112} \\ y & =112\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(112\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(112\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{\pi }{28}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =(112\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\frac{\pi }{28} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate at which the kite is gaining altitude is $4\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\,\text{ft/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields A hot air balloon $B$ is flying horizontally to the observer $O$ at a constant height of $300\,\text{m}$ above the ground. The angle of elevation $\theta $ made by the balloon and an observer is increasing at a rate of $0.05$ radians per second. What is the speed of the balloon when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/81/813a4a253bdac3c44fe66da2728ad01bf3f1db2e0612093ce8f6a81b60e50161.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the altitude of the hot air balloon, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between the balloon and the observer. The quantity $y=300\,\text{m}$ does not change with time because the hot air balloon stays at a constant altitude.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{300}{x} \\ x & =300\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(300\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=0.05$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})(0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-300(2)^{2}(0.05) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-60.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the speed of the hot air balloon is $60\,\text{m/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-0708b89d-7f7a-5637-8493-1ca6f099288c"] A park ranger $P$ stands $900\,\text{ft}$ away from the base of a lookout tower $T$ to track a drone $D$ that is ascending vertically. The angle of elevation $\theta $ formed by the ranger and the drone is increasing at a rate of $\frac{\pi }{60}$ radians per second. In the figure, $x$ is the distance between the ranger and the drone's takeoff position, and $y$ is the altitude of the drone. The quantity $x=900\,\text{ft}$ does not change with time because the distance between the ranger and the takeoff position is fixed.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{900} \\ y & =900\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(900\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =900{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{\pi }{60}$ and $\theta ={45}^{∘}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =900{sec}^{2}⁡({45}^{∘})(\frac{\pi }{60}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =900{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{60}) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =30\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the drone's altitude is increasing at a rate of $30\pi \,\text{ft/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d870faa5-187d-5160-bfd1-02d58f3d6875"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d870faa5-187d-5160-bfd1-02d58f3d6875" :answer-field/id #uuid "d870faa5-187d-5160-bfd1-02d58f3d6875" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-c15fca13-90c5-5a81-bbbf-80c06db848a3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c15fca13-90c5-5a81-bbbf-80c06db848a3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c15fca13-90c5-5a81-bbbf-80c06db848a3" :answer/id #uuid "c15fca13-90c5-5a81-bbbf-80c06db848a3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "30\pi" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-419bbacd-9dab-5629-96fc-19c329c4d054" :question/id #uuid "419bbacd-9dab-5629-96fc-19c329c4d054" :question/math-academy-id "q-2910" :question/problem "![](images/a5/a51d0d8ef1be2e7fc06aa34fe1440e77a79d8bee654703c1e931332390741c32.png)

A $13\,\text{ft}$ ladder leans against the side of a building, forming an angle $\theta $ with the ground. Given that the foot of the ladder $F$ is being pulled away from the building at the rate of $0.5\,\text{ft/s}$, at what rate is $\theta $ decreasing at the moment when the top of the ladder $T$ is $12\,\text{ft}$ above the ground?" :question/worked-solution "![](images/7b/7b923b76e90d665a722643684ce94fff50500a7be8b70aa821410a7969e4bb79.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance from the foot of the ladder to the wall of the building, $y$ is the vertical distance between the top of the ladder and the ground, and $z$ is the length of the ladder. The quantity $z=13$ feet does not change with time because the ladder's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $y=12$ feet. To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{13} \\ x & =13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.5.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}0.5 & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ -\frac{1}{26} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{26}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{12}{13} \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  & =\frac{13}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=-\frac{1}{26}\cdot \frac{13}{12}=-\frac{1}{24}.
$$

So, the angle $\theta $ is *decreasing* at a rate of $\frac{1}{24}$ radians per second." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields A lifeguard $L$ is watching a weather balloon $W$ rise vertically from a point $S$ on the beach. The point $S$ is $10\,\text{m}$ away from the lifeguard. If the balloon is rising at a constant speed of $1\,\text{m/s},$ determine the rate at which the angle of elevation $\theta $ formed by the lifeguard and the balloon is increasing at the moment when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Do not round the answer.

The angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/b4/b4b48ffa8202e15042190b98b8fc11bb02bc06547abcfbfba87b1433e5161d9b.png)

  

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance between the lifeguard and the point on the beach directly beneath the balloon, and $y$ is the balloon's height. The quantity $x=10\,\text{m}$ does not change with time because the lifeguard does not move.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{10} \\ y & =10\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =10{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =10{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =10{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =10\cdot \frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =\frac{40}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{40}\,\text{rad/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ea67d905-4e13-5fb0-9a4b-c810c57cacc6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ea67d905-4e13-5fb0-9a4b-c810c57cacc6" :answer-field/id #uuid "ea67d905-4e13-5fb0-9a4b-c810c57cacc6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-6951626e-b13c-5bfd-b94e-4811c1c0288e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6951626e-b13c-5bfd-b94e-4811c1c0288e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6951626e-b13c-5bfd-b94e-4811c1c0288e" :answer/id #uuid "6951626e-b13c-5bfd-b94e-4811c1c0288e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{40}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-579cea6b-f87a-550f-8093-6a43bd1625a5" :question/id #uuid "579cea6b-f87a-550f-8093-6a43bd1625a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-86352" :question/problem "![](images/8f/8f4638863dbc6bdfbff00d20d2153bb73eb7779719bbc7235d730539cb92329e.png)

$$

$$

In the figure, $y$ is the kite's height, and $x$ is the horizontal distance between Greta and the kite. The quantity $y=150$ inches does not change with time because the kite height remains the same.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{150}{x} \\ x & =150\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(150\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-150{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-10.$ Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =(-150{csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{1}{15} & =({csc}^{2}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate at which the angle between the kite string and the horizontal is increasing is $\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{15}$ radians per second." :question/difficulty "![](images/22/2242cf493c6307d8c6f2dac778efe6f89ca4ba6f04203940076360613c8dc9b0.png)

A $13\,\text{ft}$ support pole leans against a vertical wall, forming an angle $\theta $ with the ground. The base of the pole $B$ is being pulled toward the wall at a rate of $2\,\text{ft/s}.$ At what rate is $\theta $ increasing at the moment when the top of the pole $T$ is $5\,\text{ft}$ above the ground? Do not round the answer.

The angle is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/e0/e08cddcde0d709ebe455b8d8935174955798b877f054dab0de74d06035accc91.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance from the base of the pole to the wall, $y$ is the vertical distance between the top of the pole and the ground, and $z$ is the length of the pole. The quantity $z=13$ feet does not change with time because the pole's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $y=5$ feet. To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{13} \\ x & =13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-2$ (negative because the horizontal distance is decreasing). Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{2}{13} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{13}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{5}{13} \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  & =\frac{13}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{13}\cdot \frac{13}{5}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

So, the angle is increasing at a rate of $\frac{2}{5}\,\text{rad/s}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-af64dd03-c64b-5792-87c8-369472ee1a77"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-af64dd03-c64b-5792-87c8-369472ee1a77" :answer-field/id #uuid "af64dd03-c64b-5792-87c8-369472ee1a77" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-2fa527cb-58ec-5808-8a78-746b3d613e7b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2fa527cb-58ec-5808-8a78-746b3d613e7b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2fa527cb-58ec-5808-8a78-746b3d613e7b" :answer/id #uuid "2fa527cb-58ec-5808-8a78-746b3d613e7b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065387 :tutorial/content "Suppose that a jet takes off and climbs with an angle of $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ radians to the horizontal. The speed of the jet is $462\,\text{km}/\text{h}$ and the angle of elevation does not change. How fast is the altitude of the jet increasing?

Let's begin by drawing a diagram depicting the given information.

![](images/70/708ba0a80dd7c8e3e58e1456ad643338a8e630ec45aedb8955b042ddac92c329.png)

In the figure, $y$ is the jet's height from the ground (i.e., its altitude), $z$ is the jet's distance from its take-off point. The quantity that we're required to calculate is

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t}.
$$

To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $y$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6},$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \frac{1}{2} & =\frac{y}{z} \\ y & =\frac{1}{2}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}z) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We know that $\dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} = 462\,\textrm{km/h},$ so plugging this into the above gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 462 = 231.
$$

Therefore, the altitude is increasing at a rate of $231\,\textrm{km/h}.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065388 :tutorial/content "Consider a $2\,\text{m}$ ladder that leans against a wall, forming an angle $\theta$ with the ground. The bottom of the ladder is pushed toward the wall at a rate of $\dfrac 1 2 \,\text{m}/\text{s},$ as shown below. How fast is the angle $\theta$ increasing?

Let's begin by drawing a figure according to the given information.

![](images/16/16996176a8557dc71fe3f3a3e0d2a0c91e5b164b9eeeeeb6cf76b44952642a47.png)

In the figure,  $z$ is the length of the ladder and $x$ the distance of the bottom of the ladder from the wall. The quantity $z=2$ does not change with time because the length of the ladder is fixed.

Our job is to calculate

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d \theta}{\textrm d t}.
$$

To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta,$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{x}{2}) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the bottom of the ladder is pushed against the wall at a rate of $\dfrac 1 2 \,\text{m}/\text{s},$ we have $\dfrac{\textrm dx}{\textrm d t} = \dfrac{1}{2},$ and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064455 :activity/expected-seconds 1440.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129161 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1d879b56-35ea-5e82-93d4-20d74ef5904c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-1d879b56-35ea-5e82-93d4-20d74ef5904c" :question/id #uuid "1d879b56-35ea-5e82-93d4-20d74ef5904c" :question/math-academy-id "q-71580" :question/problem "Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{8}{x-2y+3z}?$" :question/worked-solution "The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{8}{x-2y+3z} & =c \\ 8 & =c(x-2y+3z) \\ cx-2cy+3cz-8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)$ can't be zero. Therefore, we get a family of planes:

$$
cx-2cy+3cz-8=0,\,c\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty ).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-68ec3658-a0f2-5681-81c6-416ad622e049"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that the given curve is $\text{bounded}$ (and closed), representing $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{clockwise}.$

But we have that:

- ${e}^{at}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty $ when $a>0,$ and

- ${e}^{at}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty $ when $a<0.$

Thus, we must have $a=0.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-43cb95e9-51cf-599a-bd5e-a3c29f1f9c2d" We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
2xz+2yz+xy=48.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=48
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $xyz=0,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z\ne 0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz+2yz+xy & =48 \\ 4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =48 \\ 12{z}^{2} & =48 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(4,4,2),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(4,4,2)=4\cdot 4\cdot 2=32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,5.5) & =2\cdot 2\cdot 5.5 \\  & =22 \\  & <f(4,4,2).\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186399343 :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$

$$

$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$

$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=2\lambda x \\ xz=2\lambda y \\ xy=2\lambda z\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

As we found previously, the slope is $m=-\frac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+b \\ 1 & =-(\frac{1}{3})(4)+b \\ 1 & =-\frac{4}{3}+b \\ 1+\frac{4}{3} & =b \\ b & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-249d3757-eb22-5461-8905-b54111d72bd7" "answer-field-134b35bc-2fdc-55d1-875e-ea8fc777f10d"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-249d3757-eb22-5461-8905-b54111d72bd7" :answer-field/id #uuid "249d3757-eb22-5461-8905-b54111d72bd7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f31d8396-8c45-5a1c-8211-0e6b56b99240" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f31d8396-8c45-5a1c-8211-0e6b56b99240"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f31d8396-8c45-5a1c-8211-0e6b56b99240" :answer/id #uuid "f31d8396-8c45-5a1c-8211-0e6b56b99240" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-134b35bc-2fdc-55d1-875e-ea8fc777f10d" :answer-field/id #uuid "134b35bc-2fdc-55d1-875e-ea8fc777f10d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-8d240067-2b7d-5da0-8ced-35c460f862bc" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8d240067-2b7d-5da0-8ced-35c460f862bc"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d240067-2b7d-5da0-8ced-35c460f862bc" :answer/id #uuid "8d240067-2b7d-5da0-8ced-35c460f862bc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068926 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0bc94237-c7e5-59e2-b81f-4ca609b2837a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0bc94237-c7e5-59e2-b81f-4ca609b2837a" :question/id #uuid "0bc94237-c7e5-59e2-b81f-4ca609b2837a" :question/math-academy-id "q-167073" :question/problem "Calculate the $x$-intercept of the line $\overset{↔}{AB}.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Since parallel lines have equal slopes, the slope of the new line should be equal to the slope of the line $\overset{↔}{AB},$ i.e.,

$$
m=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, we want a line with the slope $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ that passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(3,-2).$ 

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (x-3) \\ y+2 & =-\frac{1}{3}x+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x-1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-44132ea1-b7c9-5842-96df-a89dcc91fc33"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-44132ea1-b7c9-5842-96df-a89dcc91fc33" :answer-field/id #uuid "44132ea1-b7c9-5842-96df-a89dcc91fc33" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ca9f6489-52e9-5751-9fa8-55e469b75710" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ca9f6489-52e9-5751-9fa8-55e469b75710"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ca9f6489-52e9-5751-9fa8-55e469b75710" :answer/id #uuid "ca9f6489-52e9-5751-9fa8-55e469b75710" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{3}x-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175923 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c73684cd-cbd4-53ce-a02e-b8f120478413"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c73684cd-cbd4-53ce-a02e-b8f120478413" :question/id #uuid "c73684cd-cbd4-53ce-a02e-b8f120478413" :question/math-academy-id "q-167076" :question/problem "Write the equation of the line that passes through the point $(2,8)$ and is perpendicular to $\overset{↔}{AB}.$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other. Therefore, since $\overset{↔}{AB}$ has the slope $m=-\frac{1}{3},$ our perpendicular line must have a slope of 

$$

$$

So, our perpendicular line has the slope ${m}_{1}=3$ and passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,8).$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}_{1}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =3(x-2) \\ y-8 & =3x-6 \\ y & =3x+2\end{aligned}

}_{k=1}^{q}\frac{({z}_{k}+{z}_{k-1})}{2}Δ{z}_{k}.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the constant multiple rule, we can write the summation as

$$
{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}\frac{({z}_{k}+{z}_{k-1})}{2}Δ{z}_{k}=\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}({z}_{k}+{z}_{k-1})Δ{z}_{k}.
$$

We can simplify the summation as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}({z}_{k}+{z}_{k-1})Δ{z}_{k} & =({z}_{1}+{z}_{0})Δ{z}_{1}+({z}_{2}+{z}_{1})Δ{z}_{2}+⋯+({z}_{q}+{z}_{q-1})Δ{z}_{n} \\  & =({z}_{1}+{z}_{0})({z}_{1}-{z}_{0})+({z}_{2}+{z}_{1})({z}_{2}-{z}_{1})+⋯+({z}_{q}+{z}_{q-1})({z}_{q}-{z}_{q-1}) \\  & =({z}_{1}^{2}-{z}_{0}^{2})+({z}_{2}^{2}-{z}_{1}^{2})+⋯+({z}_{q}^{2}-{z}_{q-1}^{2}) \\  & =(\cancel{{z}_{1}^{2}}-{z}_{0}^{2})+(\cancel{{z}_{2}^{2}}-\cancel{{z}_{1}^{2}})+⋯+({z}_{q}^{2}-\cancel{{z}_{q-1}^{2}}) \\  & =-{z}_{0}^{2}+{z}_{q}^{2} \\  & ={z}_{q}^{2}-{z}_{0}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${z}_{0}=2$ and ${z}_{q}=6$ are the endpoints of our partition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}({z}_{k}+{z}_{k-1})Δ{z}_{k} & ={z}_{q}^{2}-{z}_{0}^{2} \\  & ={6}^{2}-{2}^{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we have

$$
\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{k=1}^{q}({z}_{k}+{z}_{k-1})Δ{z}_{k}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 32=16.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e8508966-666d-5767-9f3e-6f1a14747298"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-10bae273-6993-5b75-9a9e-139dcefc8633" :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162360 :question/problem "A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $5,$ $3,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $5,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=5\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{5}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{5}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186412767 :question/problem "A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $11$ and $4,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $11,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}=11\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=\sqrt{11}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{11}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186369741 :question/problem "A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=8,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=2\sqrt{5},$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse." :question/worked-solution "The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\{x\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse $\{Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1\}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=8,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={8}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax{‖}^{2}\}={8}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}\{‖Ax‖\}=8.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=8.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186269244 :question/problem "![](images/d4/d4947e37239d2ac2950b536d7afc2d0810ea713c437b7095a43e123d50ff2b34.png)

Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ what are the nonzero singular values of $A?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=8={\sigma }_{1},$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=5={\sigma }_{2}.$

Therefore, the nonzero singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=8$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=5.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186383431 :question/problem "![](images/63/63d5de8c08559ecc88b4fd7e2184204a1e6ea2f8a9e8ca6af7959e2354876e3f.png)

Consider a sample of size $n=80$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. *Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*"] [17592186172323 :question/worked-solution "Since $n=80$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.75,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=80\cdot 0.7=56>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=80\cdot (1-0.7)=24>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$

| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0,7\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{800}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.042\end{aligned}

["question-76598254-2f11-555f-8a0a-b51f61e7748b" :question/problem "Olivia and Harper are musicians. In the previous season, the decimal proportion of Olivia’s performances that were solos was $0.55,$ while $40%$ of Harper’s performances were solos. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. Less than half of Olivia's performances were solos.

II. More than half of Harper's performances were solos.

III. Olivia had a greater percentage of solo performances compared to Harper."] ["question-76598254-2f11-555f-8a0a-b51f61e7748b" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, since 

$$
0.55>0.5,
$$

more than half of Olivia's performances were solos.

- Statement II is false. Notice that 

$$
40%<50%.
$$

So, less than half of Harper's performances were solos.

- Statement III is true. We can compare $0.55$ and $40%$ by converting the decimal into a percent. 

To do this, we multiply it by $100:$

$$
0.55\times 100=55%
$$

Since $55%>40%,$ Olivia had a **greater** percentage of solo performances compared to Harper.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."] ["question-76598254-2f11-555f-8a0a-b51f61e7748b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-e6aac269-3443-59ce-abcc-30a3070cf5de" $$

$$

Next, we carry out the subtraction:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & \,\,\, & \,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,4\,\,\, & \,\,\,8\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,-\,\,\,\, &  & \,\,\,2\,\,\, & \,\,\,3\,\,\, \\  &  & \,\,\,2\,\,\, & \,\,\,5\,\,\,\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
48-23=25.
$$

However, since our answer must be negative, we need to change the sign of the answer above. 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$

$$

That means that there are $\frac{1}{3}$ slices of Mark's share for each slice of James' share."] [17592186074427 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186072800 :answer-field/correct 17592186072804] ["question-a8e40c21-fa80-544c-8d3a-4f03c8add411" :question/id #uuid "a8e40c21-fa80-544c-8d3a-4f03c8add411"] ["question-a8e40c21-fa80-544c-8d3a-4f03c8add411" :question/math-academy-id "q-85400"] ["question-a8e40c21-fa80-544c-8d3a-4f03c8add411" :question/problem "Which of the following numbers are divisible by $9?$

I. $7\,050\,113$

II. $5\,119\,232$

III. $14\,624\,100$"] ["question-a8e40c21-fa80-544c-8d3a-4f03c8add411" :question/worked-solution "A number is divisible by $9$ if the sum of its digits is divisible by $9.$

- The sum of the digits of $7\,050\,113$ is

$$
7+0+5+0+1+1+3=17,
$$

which is *not* divisible by $9.$ So, $7\,050\,113$ is *not* divisible by $9.$

- The sum of the digits of $5\,119\,232$ is

$$
5+1+1+9+2+3+2=23,
$$

which is *not* divisible by $9.$ So, $5\,119\,232$ is *not* divisible by $9.$

- The sum of the digits of $14\,624\,100$ is

$$
1+4+6+2+4+1+0+0=18,
$$

which is divisible by $9.$ So, $14\,624\,100$ is divisible by $9.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "llI only.""] ["question-a8e40c21-fa80-544c-8d3a-4f03c8add411" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7f142419-33c2-52ed-b329-1e3e4574c8cf" {{field-1}} $\text{ m/s}.$"] ["question-7cce7dd9-a52f-5429-96fd-d564ac81f3b8" :question/worked-solution "Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is one third of the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{1}{3}h \\ 2r & =\frac{1}{3}h \\ r & =\frac{1}{6}h.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}\pi  & =\frac{1}{36}\pi (6)^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height is always three times its base diameter. So, we have $h=3r.$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}(3r) \\  & =\pi {r}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =3\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

A beverage is pumped into a conical dispenser at a constant rate of  $19.6\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.$ The mouth of the tank is $70\,\text{cm}$ in diameter and the height of the tank is $40\,\text{cm}.$ How fast is the beverage level increasing when the volume of the beverage in the dispenser is $12.25\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}?$ Round your answer to two decimal places."] ["question-e05d5196-22d0-5390-9d3c-413318bc7364" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the tank. Let's call $H=40\,\text{cm}$ the height of the tank, and $R=\frac{70}{2}=35\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the solution level. We call $h$ the solution level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the solution. Both of these quantities, and the solution volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=19.6\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $v=12.25\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the tank and the solution must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{35}{40} \\ r & =\frac{7h}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{7h}{8})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{49}{192}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$

Let's call $H=6\,\text{cm}$ the height of the cup, and $R=2\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=3\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the cup and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{2}{6} \\ r & =\frac{h}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{3})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{9}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =\frac{1}{9}\pi ({3}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -2 & =\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm/s}.$"] ["question-829ceea0-b4f0-5bef-b797-d4b161d8e247" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] How fast is the beverage level dropping when there is $576\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}$ of beverage remaining in the funnel?"] ["question-f35215fb-23bc-5523-aa38-ea3ed45464a8" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the funnel. Let's call $H=50\,\text{cm}$ the height of the funnel, and $R=50\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-16\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $v=576\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the funnel and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{50}{50} \\ r & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(h)}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the level of water in the funnel is changing when $v=576\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}576\pi  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3} \\ {h}^{3} & =1\,728 \\ h & =12\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values into the formula for $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-16\pi  & =\pi (12)^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -16 & =144\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the beverage level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{9}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}.$"] ["question-f35215fb-23bc-5523-aa38-ea3ed45464a8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] $$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{8}{15} \\ r & =\frac{8}{15}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{8}{15}h)}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{64}{675}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{64}{675}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{64}{225}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the volume of water in the cup is changing when $h=10\,\text{m}.$ 
So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{64}{225}\pi (10)^{2}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & ≈28.4\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{h}\end{aligned}
$$

A container has the shape of a right circular cone. The height of the container is $20\,\text{in}$ and the diameter at the top of the container is $10\,\text{in}.$ Water in the container is evaporating so that its depth, $h$, is decreasing at a constant rate of $\frac{10}{3}\,\text{in/h}.$ At what rate is the volume of water decreasing when the water depth is $12\,\text{in}?$"] ["question-a9bed4a9-ed2b-5603-85e6-df6b8285a648" :question/worked-solution "First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=20\,\text{in}$ the height of the conical container, and $R=\frac{10}{2}=5\,\text{in}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the height of the water and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{10}{3}\,\text{in}/\text{h},
$$

and we want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=12\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the water must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{5}{20} \\ r & =\frac{h}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{4})}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{1}{48}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{48}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{16}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the volume of water in the container is changing when $h=12\,\text{in}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{16}\pi (12)^{2}(-\frac{10}{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-30\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of water is decreasing at a rate of $30\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h}.$"] ["question-a9bed4a9-ed2b-5603-85e6-df6b8285a648" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "question-0c589335-1cfb-54d8-9a5c-d454270a6ef5"] [17592186065389 :tutorial/content "We can use differentiation to solve related rates problems in the context of cones. In general, we follow the usual three steps:

**Step 1:** Draw a diagram and identify the variables that change with time.

**Step 2:** Write down a relation between the time-dependent variables.

**Step 3:** Differentiate the relation with respect to time and plug in the known values.

Before we start, recall that the volume $v$ of a right cone of radius $r$ and height $h$ (shown below) is given by the formula

$$
v = \dfrac13 \pi r^2 h.
$$

![](images/cf/cf4e3b5b9f0d827bccaee008e006ad62d870fb2d782df8dd94f61bc4a3ca4050.png)"] [17592186065330 :step/math-academy-id 631140] [17592186065180 :step/math-academy-id 631141] [17592186065331 :step/math-academy-id 631145] [17592186065179 :step/math-academy-id 631148] [17592186065332 :step/math-academy-id 631153] [17592186064437 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0] [17592186362337 :question/worked-solution "We must find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-1=2\lambda x \\ -1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1$ and solve for $\lambda ,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4{\lambda }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\ \frac{2}{4{\lambda }^{2}} & =1 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \lambda  & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $x$ and $y.$ This gives

$$
x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\,y=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}),\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $\,(x,y)\,$ | $\,(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\,$ | $\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}})\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $\,1+\sqrt{2}\,$ | $\,1-\sqrt{2}\,$ |

:question/id #uuid "a5878b34-7fd0-5b9f-89d8-91c764ed89b8"] ["question-a5878b34-7fd0-5b9f-89d8-91c764ed89b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-70552"] ["question-a5878b34-7fd0-5b9f-89d8-91c764ed89b8" :question/problem "Determine the vertical asymptotes of $f(x)=\frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}-1}.$"] ["question-a5878b34-7fd0-5b9f-89d8-91c764ed89b8" :question/worked-solution "To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x-1}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{x-1}{(x+1)(x-1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x-1}}{(x+1)\cancel{(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
x+1=0
$$

This gives the solution $x=-1.$ Therefore, $x=-1$ is the only vertical asymptote."] ["question-a5878b34-7fd0-5b9f-89d8-91c764ed89b8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-1)^{2}-4(1)(2) \\  & =1-8 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

:question/answer-fields "answer-field-bc072fa3-a3a2-5452-b980-3ee1ebbabe24"] [17592186088921 :tutorial/content "A **vertical asymptote** is a vertical line to which a function gets very close but never touches.

For example, let's consider the rational function 

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{1}{(x-2)(x+2)}.
$$

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/79/79e02370d60aec1e1e7f9e21dafbb876ea1f9b9b2de2b3d2b8b6ba14ffabfe3d.png)

The two dotted lines $x=2$ and $x=-2$ are the vertical asymptotes of the function. The function gets closer and closer to these lines but never touches them.

But how can we calculate the vertical asymptotes of a function without using a graph?

In general, we can find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function using the following procedure:

1\. Factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors.

2\. Set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x .$

In our case, the function is already factored, and there are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. So, to find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x{:}$

$$
(x-2)(x+2) = 0
$$

The solutions to this equation are $x=2$ and $x=-2.$  Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ This matches up with what we saw in the graph."] [17592186087895 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0] [17592186171848 :question/problem "A fair die has $12$ sides labeled with numbers $1$ through $12.$ What is the expected value of a random roll of this die?"] [17592186171848 :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the number the die lands on. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U \{1, 2, \ldots, 12\},$ and we wish to compute $\textrm E[X].$

In general, if $X \sim U \{a, a + 1, \ldots, b\},$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U \{ 1, 2, \ldots, 12\},$ we have the following expected value:

$$
\textrm E[X] = \dfrac{1+12}{2} = 6.5
$$

Therefore, the expected value is $6.5.$"] [17592186171849 :question/problem "A fair die has sides labeled with numbers $4$ through $15.$ What is the variance of the numbers obtained when rolling this die?"] [17592186171849 :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the number the die lands on. From the problem statement, we know that $X \sim U \{ 4, 5, \ldots, 15 \},$ and we wish to compute $\textrm{Var}[X].$

In general, if $X \sim U \{a, a + 1, \ldots, b\},$ then the variance of $X$ is

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{|S|^2-1}{12}
$$

where $S = \{a, a+1, \ldots, b\}.$

Now, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}|S| & =b-a+1 \\  & =15-4+1 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X \sim U \{ 4, 5, \ldots, 15 \},$ we have the following variance:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{12^2 - 1}{12} = \dfrac{143}{12}
$$

Therefore, the variance is $\dfrac{143}{12}.$"] ["question-061c757d-590b-5605-a6a4-5e9539c29dc6" :question/id #uuid "061c757d-590b-5605-a6a4-5e9539c29dc6"] ["question-061c757d-590b-5605-a6a4-5e9539c29dc6" :question/math-academy-id "q-149461"] ["question-061c757d-590b-5605-a6a4-5e9539c29dc6" :question/problem "In summer, the daily maximum temperature in a particular city (rounded to the nearest degree) varies between ${25}^{∘}C$ and ${36}^{∘}C,$ inclusive. Assuming that each maximum temperature value has the same probability of occurring on a given summer day, what is the expected value of the daily maximum temperature?"] ["question-061c757d-590b-5605-a6a4-5e9539c29dc6" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the daily maximum temperature (rounded to the nearest degree) on a randomly selected day. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U\{25,26,…,36\},$ and we wish to compute $\text{E}[X].$

In general, if $X∼U\{a,a+1,…,b\},$ then $X$ has the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{a+b}{2}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U\{25,26,…,36\},$ we have the following expected value:

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{25+36}{2}=30.5
$$

Therefore, the expected value of the maximum temperature is ${30.5}^{∘}C.$"] ["question-061c757d-590b-5605-a6a4-5e9539c29dc6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] :question/problem "A traditional festival is usually held on a single day after the $6$th and before the $15$th of September. The exact day is selected each year and depends on the weather conditions. Assuming that each day after the $6$th and before the $15$th of September has the same probability of being chosen, what is the standard deviation of the selected days? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places."] ["question-1e997cfb-3847-52d2-9127-67ab63d15dde" :question/worked-solution "Let $X$ represent the date of the selected day. From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U\{7,8,…,14\},$ and we wish to compute $\text{SD}[X].$

In general, if $X∼U\{a,a+1,…,b\},$ then the variance of $X$ is

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{|S{|}^{2}-1}{12}
$$

where $S=\{a,a+1,…,b\}.$

Now, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}|S| & =b-a+1 \\  & =14-7+1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U\{7,8,…,14\},$ we have the following variance:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{{8}^{2}-1}{12}=\frac{63}{12}
$$

Finally,

$$

From the problem statement, we know that $X∼U\{0,1,…,9\},$ and we wish to compute $\text{SD}[X].$

In general, if $X∼U\{a,a+1,…,b\},$ then the variance of $X$ is

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{|S{|}^{2}-1}{12}
$$

where $S=\{a,a+1,…,b\}.$

Now, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}|S| & =b-a+1 \\  & =9-0+1 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our random variable $X∼U\{0,1,…,9\},$ we have the following variance:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\frac{{10}^{2}-1}{12}=\frac{99}{12}
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SD}[X]=\sqrt{\frac{99}{12}}≈2.87.
$$"] ["question-2200f2ed-00f4-5dc2-a53c-43c556e4cd84" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3cf40b77-3ab5-59b6-90e4-0f17d078e3d7" :answer-field/id #uuid ![](images/0a/0abfcf5eccaaaf22dbc144f58098d394297a5819a1857ff316ce9e9d01e44f7d.svg)

Let's now suppose that 

$$
X\sim U\{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b\},
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are integers. In other words, we're concerned with the special case where the support $S$ of $X$ contains every integer between $a$ and $b$ inclusive. 

In this case, it can be shown that the mean value of $X$ is given by

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}.
$$

It can also be shown that

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{|S|^2-1}{12}.
$$

We'll prove these results at the end of the lesson."] [17592186173221 :tutorial/content "Here, we will show that for $X\sim \{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b\},$ we have

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{a+b}{2}.
$$

First, recall that the probability mass function of $X$ is given by

![](images/36/36e73322640df22386428fdc41d1940ef7469587566c2f4f24936158292c087c.svg)

By the definition of expected value for discrete random variables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}xf(x) \\  & ={\sum }_{x\in S}x\cdot \frac{1}{|S|} \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}{\sum }_{x\in S}x \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}[a+(a+1)+(a+2)+⋯+b].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the term in the square brackets is an arithmetic series with the first term $a$ and the last term $b.$ Therefore, using the formula for the sum of an arithmetic series, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =\frac{1}{|S|}[a+(a+1)+(a+2)+⋯+b] \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot \frac{|S|}{2}\cdot (a+b) \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{|S|}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{|S|}}{2}\cdot (a+b) \\  & =\frac{a+b}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

as required."] [17592186173222 :tutorial/content "Let's now show that for $X\sim \{a, a+1, a+2, \ldots, b\},$ we have

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \dfrac{|S|^2-1}{12}.
$$

We will assume, without loss of generality, that the distribution of our random variable $X$ is given by

$$
X\sim\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, |S|\}.
$$

We do not lose generality here because, in general, the variance (i.e., spread) of a random variable is unaffected by translations:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X + c] = \textrm{Var}[X]
$$

  

By the definition of $\textrm{E}[X^2],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}f(x) \\  & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{|S|} \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot {\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot [{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+⋯+|S{|}^{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

We now make use of the following result:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n i^2 = \dfrac16 n (n+1)(2n+1)
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot [{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+⋯+|S{|}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{|S|}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\cdot |S|\cdot (|S|+1)(2|S|+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{|S|}}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\cdot \cancel{|S|}\cdot (|S|+1)(2|S|+1) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we use the following results:

$$
\textrm{Var}[X] = \textrm{E}[X^2] - \left(\textrm{E}[X]\right)^2, \qquad \textrm {E}[X] = \dfrac{1+|S|}{2}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-{(\text{E}[X])}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}-{(\frac{|S|+1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{6}-\frac{(|S|+1)^{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{2(|S|+1)(2|S|+1)}{12}-\frac{3(|S|+1)^{2}}{12} \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(2(2|S|+1)-3(|S|+1)) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(4|S|+2-3|S|-3) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)}{12}(|S|-1) \\  & =\frac{(|S|+1)(|S|-1)}{12} \\  & =\frac{|S{|}^{2}-1}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
f=-2\operatorname{coth}⁡g,\,g=4x
$$

The chain rule states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}\cdot \frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}g}=2{csch}^{2}\,g,
$$

and

$$
\frac{\text{d}g}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

Finally, multiplying the two results together and substituting for $g$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2{csch}^{2}⁡g\cdot 4 \\  & =8{csch}^{2}⁡g \\  & =8{csch}^{2}⁡4x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c4169769-2e08-50ac-8627-9cd65f653a9b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-d79f42f3-7a3e-5cfc-ae54-7f17a62555f4" :answer-field/id #uuid
